what: Build Check Part 1 (ROC Operations Manual §14.2A): every source the Source Register lists for a finding was reopened on 6 October 2026 and each recorded quotation looked for on its page. 'also_says' lists further sentences the checkers confirmed on the same pages.

checks.recorded: "Pruning starts up north around early July while in the colder parts of the South Island, it gets under-way in August."
checks.page_wording: Pruning starts up north around early July while in the colder parts of the South Island, it gets under-way in August.
checks.note: Word for word, under the question 'When is the best time to prune your roses in New Zealand?', after 'Depends on where you live.' It contrasts 'up north' (early July) with 'the colder parts of the South Island' (August), so later where colder. The page never mentions frost or 'milder/frosty districts'; that wording is not from this page.

checks.recorded: "Peak bloom in spring is first two weeks in November for the upper North Island, last two weeks for the lower North Island"
checks.page_wording: Peak bloom in spring is first two weeks in November for the upper North Island, last two weeks for the lower North Island and...
checks.note: Word for word; the recorded fragment stops before the South Island part, but the full sentence does give all three areas. It is about when to see roses in flower (visitor question), not about pruning or care timing. The next sentence adds that there are regional variations and each season differs.

checks.recorded: "Pruning starts up north around early July"
checks.page_wording: Pruning starts up north around early July while in the colder parts of the South Island, it gets under-way in August.
checks.note: The page supports only the start: pruning 'starts up north around early July'. It gives no end date for the north; 'to early August' is not on this page. 'Up north' is not defined.

checks.recorded: "in the colder parts of the South Island, it gets under-way in August."
checks.page_wording: Pruning starts up north around early July while in the colder parts of the South Island, it gets under-way in August.
checks.note: Supports 'colder parts of the South Island ... gets under-way in August' (a start month). The page does not say 'or later', does not mention frost or 'once the worst frosts have passed', and does not name inland or frost-prone districts.

checks.recorded: "Winter is the best time to plant as it allows the plant to establish before summer arrives."
checks.page_wording: Winter is the best time to plant as it allows the plant to establish before summer arrives.
checks.note: Word for word under 'When can I plant roses?'. Supports winter as the best planting time for roses generally (New Zealand as a whole). The page does not say 'bare-root', names no months (no June to August), and does not mention Canterbury; its spring/summer remark is about potted roses only.

checks.recorded: "If planting potted roses during spring and summer, keep them well watered."
checks.page_wording: If planting potted roses during spring and summer, keep them well watered.
checks.note: Word for word, second sentence under 'When can I plant roses?'. It supports keeping potted roses well watered if planted in spring and summer. The page does not say potted roses can be planted 'at any time of year'; that is an inference (autumn is not mentioned at all).

checks.recorded: "Your local rose society can provide advice suited to your own climate."
checks.page_wording: Your local rose society can provide advice suited to your own climate.
checks.note: Word for word, the last sentence of the answer on when to prune roses in New Zealand. In context it is advice about pruning timing for the gardener's own climate.

contradictions: Nothing on the page contradicts the findings, but it is thinner than several findings imply: no end date for northern pruning, no mention of frost anywhere, no months for planting, no use of 'bare-root', and no statement that potted roses can go in at any time of year.

checks.recorded: "Most people prune in July and even August."
checks.page_wording: Most people prune in July and even August.
checks.note: Word for word, in the PRUNING section. Supports July and August as the usual months. The page does not mention pruning in June and says nothing about regions, climate or frost, so the 'June to August' range is not from this page. Text dates from 1996.

checks.recorded: "most garden centres promote new roses early in June."
checks.page_wording: If not most garden centres promote new roses early in June.
checks.note: The fragment is word for word, in the PURCHASING section, after a sentence about roses ordered from a nursery. It says garden centres 'promote new roses early in June'; it does not say 'bare-root' and says 'promote', not arrive or reach. 1996 text; no region given.

checks.recorded: "Rake up all fallen leaves and burn them as they can harbour spores that spread disease later on."
checks.page_wording: Rake up all fallen leaves and burn them as they can harbour spores that spread disease later on.
checks.note: Word for word, in the PREPARATION section, between 'new beds should be prepared in April/May' and the June clean-up spray. Supports clearing fallen leaves in the autumn/early-winter preparation stage, but the sentence itself names no month, does not say 'at pruning', and the page does not mention Canterbury.

checks.recorded: "it is highly recommended that clean up sprays be applied in June."
checks.page_wording: In preparation for the spring, it is highly recommended that clean up sprays be applied in June.
checks.note: Fragment is word for word, in the PREPARATION section. Supports a clean-up spray in June only. The page does not say this June spray is after pruning (it sits before the July/August pruning section), and July is not named for spraying. The only spray it places after pruning is 'a post prune spray of copper and oil', with no month.

contradictions: AF-33: the June clean-up spray is given under PREPARATION, ahead of pruning ('Most people prune in July and even August'), so on this page it is not an after-pruning spray; the after-pruning spray is a separate one (copper and oil) with no month named. July is not named for spraying.
AF-33: the page does not say which type the June clean-up spray is; it only warns that lime sulphur and copper based sprays must not be used within 2 weeks of each other.
AF-32: leaf raking is listed with bed preparation, not with pruning.
The page is a 1996 text with no regional guidance at all (no north/south, no frost).

checks.recorded: "roses are usually pruned between late June and mid August depending on where you live"
checks.page_wording: Its almost rose pruning time in New Zealand ... roses are usually pruned between late June and mid August depending on where you live.
checks.note: Fragment is word for word, in the opening sentence of a 2019 news item about pruning demonstrations; it is about the main winter pruning for New Zealand as a whole. Supports the range (late June to mid August). It does not say 'most often July and August'; the only hint is that all four listed demonstrations are on 20-21 July 2019.

checks.recorded: "depending on where you live"
checks.page_wording: roses are usually pruned between late June and mid August depending on where you live.
checks.note: Word for word. Supports 'depends on where you live' for the pruning window. The page does not mention microclimate, frost or climate at all, so the microclimate half of the finding is not supported here.

contradictions: No contradiction. The page says nothing about microclimate, frost, north or south. Its demonstrations for Otago, Southland and Westland are all on 20-21 July (2019), which sits a little awkwardly with a blanket 'August or later' for the colder South Island (AF-10, not checked against this source).

also_says.quote: Feilding Saturday 20th July; Otago Saturday 20th July; Southland Sunday 21st July; Westland Saturday 20th July.
also_says.note: List of 2019 rose-society pruning demonstrations (dates as read from the page list, not one sentence); main winter pruning; all in the third week of July, including the southern South Island.

checks.recorded: "The general rule is the colder the climate, the later you prune in winter."
checks.page_wording: The general rule is the colder the climate, the later you prune in winter.
checks.note: Word for word, the second sentence of the article, straight before the Dunedin late-July sentence. It supports 'prune later where it is colder' as a general rule (main winter pruning). The page does not itself contrast north and south or name any other district; it names only Dunedin Botanic Garden.

checks.recorded: "At Dunedin Botanic Garden we prune modern roses in late July"
checks.page_wording: At Dunedin Botanic Garden we prune modern roses in late July, when they are at their most dormant and hopefully the heaviest...
checks.note: Word for word. Stated for Dunedin Botanic Garden practice and for 'modern roses' (main winter pruning); 2014 article, which also advertises a pruning demonstration on Saturday 19th July.

checks.recorded: "when they are at their most dormant and hopefully the heaviest of frosts have passed."
checks.page_wording: ...we prune modern roses in late July, when they are at their most dormant and hopefully the heaviest of frosts have passed.
checks.note: Word for word. Both signals are named: 'most dormant' and 'the heaviest of frosts have passed' (qualified by 'hopefully'). It is stated as Dunedin Botanic Garden's own practice for modern roses, not as a national rule.

contradictions: No contradiction. Note the timing sentence is limited to 'modern roses' at Dunedin Botanic Garden and the frost signal is hedged with 'hopefully'.

also_says.topic: Q5 winter spray type and timing
also_says.quote: After pruning, apply a spray of copper and oil at winter strength, spray around bud union to destroy over-wintering diseases...
also_says.note: Winter spray after the main pruning (late July at Dunedin); type copper and oil; sentence continues 'and insect eggs that tend to hide at the base' (one of three readings stopped at 'diseases').

checks.recorded: "at Dunedin Botanic Garden pruning is left until late July, after the worst of the frosts."
checks.page_wording: ...so at Dunedin Botanic Garden pruning is left until late July, after the worst of the frosts.
checks.note: Word for word. The full sentence begins 'Modern roses are pruned hard and low to the ground, leaving them vulnerable to frost, so...', so late July is for modern (bush) roses at Dunedin Botanic Garden. The same page says old fashioned roses had already been pruned over the past month.

checks.recorded: "If pruned too early, roses can be hit by frost but too late and growth will have already started."
checks.page_wording: If pruned too early, roses can be hit by frost but too late and growth will have already started.
checks.note: Word for word, after 'Knowing your garden is key to judging timing.' It supports 'pruning too early risks frost damage'. It does not say that new growth is what gets damaged: the page's stated reason is that modern roses pruned hard and low are left 'vulnerable to frost'. Stated in a Dunedin article, not as a national rule.

contradictions: AF-15: the page gives the frost risk as hard-pruned, low plants being 'vulnerable to frost', not as frost damage to new growth; no sentence on the page links new growth to frost.
AF-11: late July is for modern roses only; old fashioned roses 'over the past month' (before 9 July) were already being pruned, because they are pruned higher and are 'less vulnerable to frosts'.

also_says.topic: Q8 go by your own garden
also_says.quote: Knowing your garden is key to judging timing.
also_says.note: Main winter pruning; general statement in a Dunedin article, directly before the too-early/too-late sentence.

also_says.quote: Different locations can have different conditions, even pockets within the same suburb, so observe your own garden to decide exactly when is best.
also_says.note: Main winter pruning timing; Dunedin article; follows the too-early/too-late sentence.

also_says.quote: It is the ideal time to plant new roses, and prune existing ones.
also_says.note: 'It' is winter ('Over winter there is plenty to keep a rose gardener busy.'); article dated 9 July, Dunedin; no months named. A later sentence gives a planting method for 'bare-rooted roses' without a month.

also_says.topic: Q1 old fashioned roses pruned earlier
also_says.quote: ...over the past month, we have been pruning the old fashioned roses, just to shape and tidy them...
also_says.note: Dunedin Botanic Garden, article dated 9 July, so roughly June to early July; sentence continues 'they are pruned higher than the moderns so are less vulnerable to frosts'.

checks.recorded: "frosty locations can mean waiting until mid-August."
checks.page_wording: Take into consideration the microclimate in your garden, though, as frosty locations can mean waiting until mid-August.
checks.note: Fragment is word for word. Supports waiting until mid-August in 'frosty locations' (main winter pruning), said about garden microclimate in a Dunedin article. It does not say 'August or later', does not name the colder South Island or inland districts, and does not use the words 'once the worst frosts have passed'. 'Until mid-August' reads as an upper limit.

checks.recorded: "Roses need pruning when they are at their most dormant, which in Dunedin tends to be late July."
checks.page_wording: Roses need pruning when they are at their most dormant, which in Dunedin tends to be late July.
checks.note: Word for word. Main winter pruning; stated for Dunedin, hedged with 'tends to be'; the signal named is 'most dormant'. Article dated 5 July 2018 and promotes a demonstration on 21 July, mainly for modern roses.

checks.recorded: "Take into consideration the microclimate in your garden, though, as frosty locations can mean waiting until mid-August."
checks.page_wording: Take into consideration the microclimate in your garden, though, as frosty locations can mean waiting until mid-August.
checks.note: Word for word. Supports the microclimate half of the finding (frosty gardens wait until mid-August). The page does not say timing depends on 'where you live' and names no place other than Dunedin.

contradictions: AF-10: the page gives late July for Dunedin, a southern South Island city, and treats mid-August as the limit for frosty spots ('waiting until mid-August'), not 'August or later'. It names no inland or colder district.

also_says.quote: ...pick up all the clippings and leaves but to avoid spreading pests and diseases, don't put them in the compost.
also_says.note: Sentence begins 'When you have finished pruning,'; clear-up straight after the main winter pruning (late July in Dunedin). No spray, feeding or planting advice on the page.

checks.recorded: "Roses benefit from pruning each winter when they are not in active growth."
checks.page_wording: Roses benefit from pruning each winter when they are not in active growth.
checks.note: Word for word. Supports only a dormancy-type signal ('not in active growth') for winter pruning, on a page about roses for the Auckland region. The page does not use the words 'dormant' or 'frost' and names no month, so 'worst frosts having passed' is not supported here.

checks.recorded: "Apply fertiliser in spring to help keep plants healthy."
checks.page_wording: Always tidy up any dead and diseased fallen leaves and apply fertiliser in spring to help keep plants healthy.
checks.note: The recorded words are the second half of a longer sentence (page has lower-case 'apply'). Supports feeding in spring only. The page does not say 'as new growth appears' or 'after pruning', names no month, and gives no last feed.

checks.recorded: "Planting is best done in autumn or winter."
checks.page_wording: Planting is best done in autumn or winter.
checks.note: Word for word, in the planting advice. The page is about roses for 'the Auckland region'; the sentence itself does not repeat Auckland. The next sentence refers to plants 'in their container', so it is not specifically about bare-root roses; no months named.

contradictions: AF-14: the page never mentions frost or dormancy, and names no month for anything.
AF-18: no trigger for the first feed is given beyond 'in spring'.
The garden says it only grows roses that 'stay healthy without spraying'; no winter spray is recommended on this page.

also_says.topic: Q5 clearing fallen leaves; Q2 feeding
also_says.quote: Always tidy up any dead and diseased fallen leaves and apply fertiliser in spring to help keep plants healthy.

also_says.quote: Remove spent flowers throughout the flowering season as this will help encourage new flowers and prolong flowering.

checks.recorded: "Frosts are common in the cooler months for most of the country, however they occur rarely north of Waikato."
checks.page_wording: Frosts are common in the cooler months for most of the country, however they occur rarely north of Waikato.
checks.note: Word for word; reported as being in the Summary (about page 4) of the PDF. It is a general climate statement for New Zealand; 'cooler months' are not named as months.

checks.recorded: "they occur less frequently in coastal and northernmost areas."
checks.page_wording: Both types of frost are quite common for many New Zealand locations..., but they occur less frequently in coastal and northernmost areas.
checks.note: Fragment is word for word (Frosts subsection, about page 32). The quotation itself covers only 'less frequent in coastal and northernmost areas'. The 'most frequent inland' half is carried by a neighbouring sentence: 'both types occur most frequently at inland South Island locations such as Alexandra' (inland South Island, not inland generally).

checks.recorded: "Areas most likely to experience frost are flat areas ... and in valleys and basins."
checks.page_wording: ...areas most likely to experience frost are flat areas, where relatively cold air is not able to drain away..., and in valleys and basins...
checks.note: The recorded text (with its ellipsis) matches; the sentence starts 'Therefore, areas...' and continues after 'basins'. The quotation covers flat areas, valleys and basins; the 'local, varies widely over small areas' half is the opening sentence of the same Frosts subsection, which two separate readings found word for word.

contradictions: None found. Note 'most frequently' is said of inland South Island locations such as Alexandra, not of inland areas in general. Table values for frost days could not be read reliably through WebFetch (PDF table) and were not used.

also_says.note: First sentence of the Frosts subsection in the national document (same sentence as recorded from the Otago document).

checks.recorded: "air frosts occur most frequently at the inland location of Alexandra."
checks.page_wording: Ground frosts occur more frequently than air frosts, and air frosts occur most frequently at the inland location of Alexandra.
checks.note: Fragment is word for word (the first reading mislabelled it NEAR and quoted the wrong sentence; a second reading gave the full sentence). It covers Otago only and air frosts only: inland Alexandra has the most. It says nothing about coastal or northernmost areas of New Zealand, so it supports only the 'most frequent inland' part, for one region.

checks.recorded: "Frost is a local phenomenon and both its frequency of occurrence and intensity can vary widely over small areas."
checks.page_wording: Frost is a local phenomenon and both its frequency of occurrence and intensity can vary widely over small areas.
checks.note: Word for word (about page 29). The quotation supports 'frost is local and can vary widely over small areas'. For the second half, this document says 'flat areas ... and in valleys'; the phrase 'valleys and basins' was not found in the Otago document, so 'basins' comes only from the national document. The document covers Otago only.

Two readings of the frost-day table through WebFetch disagreed (Alexandra air frosts 12 versus 68 a year; Dunedin Musselburgh 0.4 versus 5.1), so no table figure from this PDF should be relied on without opening the PDF directly.

checks.recorded: "Annual days of ground frost across selected New Zealand locations ... Provider: NIWA"

checks.note: Title and provider are on the page; the chart data were readable as text and came out the same in two readings.
